The soils in this unit have a moderate to severe water erosion hazard. Those soils with clay, loamy sand and sandy loam surfaces are subject to moderate soil blowing. The Tullock soil with rapid permeability is subject to severe soil blowing. The Frazer, Haverson, Korchea, and Lohmiller soils are subject to stream bank erosion and occasional overflow in early spring. The Hysham soil is sodium affected and form hard surface crusts on drying. It is difficult to work and seedling emergence is retarded.
Most of these soils occur as complexes in which shallow depth makes them unsuitable for cultivation. Their main use is for range.
Capability Unit VIw Dryland
This unit consists of deep soils on floodplains, low terraces, and valley bottoms. These loam and silty clay loam soils are subject to flooding and in places have a water table within 3 feet of the surface. The permeability is slow to moderate. The available water holding capacity is 8 to 12 inches. Runoff is slow. The erosion hazard is severe during flooding.
The frost free season is 105 to 125 days. The annual precipitation is 12 to 15 inches.
The soils are suited only for range.
Capability Unit VIIe Dryland
This unit consists of shallow and moderately deep soils mixed with limestone, shale, sandstone, and porcelanite outcrops on deeply dissected highlands. Texture ranges from clay to loam. Type range includes extremely stony, channery and gravelly, Slopes are steep and very steep. The available water holding capacity is 3 to 4 inches on the shallow soils and about 6 inches on the moderately deep soils. Runoff is rapid and the erosion hazard is severe. Gully erosion is active in the drainageways. Runoff waters carry large amounts of sediment. Permeability to plant roots, water and air ranges from slow to rapid.
The frost free season is 105 to 125 days for the Midway, Thedalund, Wibaux, and Lismas soils.
These soils are used for range, game range, and recreation. Grazing management is necessary to ensure adequate plant cover.
